name: Prequalify subcontractors
summary: A general contractor that subcontracts most of its work only invites trades to bid once they have shown they are financially sound, insured, registered with the workers' compensation board and safe to have on site. Prequalification analysts send each new or renewing trade a questionnaire, chase the certificates and statements, verify the WSIB clearance online and check insurance, then a regional safety manager rates the safety record and the analyst sets a subcontract limit from the financial statements. The supply chain manager approves the limit, and the record feeds the bid lists estimators use. The process is slow because trades send incomplete or expired documents and the work waits on busy safety managers, and errors come from self-reported statistics and certificates that expire after approval.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian national general contractor with about $1.5B annual revenue, about 3,000 active subcontracts and a central supply chain team keeping the approved subcontractor list.
baseline.notes: Describes prequalification in 2019-2022 using a prequalification database or spreadsheet with emailed questionnaires; some contractors also used third-party registries such as ComplyWorks, Avetta or ISNetworld.

unit_of_work: one subcontractor prequalification, new or annual renewal
trigger: An estimator or project manager wants to invite a trade that is not on the approved list, a trade applies, or an approved trade's annual prequalification is due for renewal.
end_state: The trade is on the approved list with a limit and expiry dates, approved with conditions, or rejected with reasons recorded.

volume.seasonality: Heavier from January to April as approved trades renew after year-end statements and estimators build bid lists for the construction season.

evidence.note: About 45 to 70 new firms a month (the organisation file's 40 to 90) plus annual renewals of an approved list of roughly 700 to 1,000 active trades; the renewal count is the author's estimate from about 3,000 active subcontracts.

surge.cause: Annual renewal season after trades' fiscal year-end statements

evidence.note: Author's estimate: most trades have December year-ends and renew once statements are ready.

systems.name: Subcontractor prequalification database (questionnaires, insurance and WSIB certificates)
Government portals (WSIB clearance, Ministry of Labour notice of project, CRA, land registry)
Safety management system (hazard assessments, inspections, incidents, training records)
Reporting and dashboards (Excel cost reports, Power BI)

steps.name: Log the request and open a prequalification file
steps.description: The prequalification analyst records a new firm referred by an estimator or project manager, a firm applying on its own, or an approved firm whose annual prequalification is about to expire, and opens or updates its record in the prequalification database.
inputs: estimator referral, subcontractor enquiry or renewal reminder

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of Canadian general contractors.

steps.name: Send the questionnaire and document checklist
steps.description: The analyst sends the questionnaire link or form with the checklist of documents: financial statements, bonding letter, insurance certificates, WSIB or WCB clearance and premium rate statements, injury statistics, COR certificate, safety manual contents and references.

evidence.note: Document lists from two Canadian contractor prequalification forms; times are estimates.

steps.name: Wait for the subcontractor's submission
steps.description: The trade's office manager or owner fills in the questionnaire and gathers certificates and statements from its accountant, broker, surety and the WSIB, then uploads or emails the package.

error.defect_description: Documents missing, expired or not matching the legal entity name.

evidence.note: Subcontractors must submit the form and supporting documentation before bidding; waiting time is an estimate.

steps.name: Check the submission for completeness
steps.description: The analyst opens each attachment, checks that every required document is present, current, signed and issued to the same legal name, and that the questionnaire answers are complete.

error.defect_description: A stale certificate passes the completeness check.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of Canadian general contractors.

steps.name: Chase missing or expired documents
steps.description: The analyst emails or phones the subcontractor listing what is missing or expired (most often insurance certificates, the WSIB clearance or year-end statements) and sets a follow-up date.

evidence.note: The organisation file names expired insurance and clearance certificates as the usual gap; chase time is an estimate.

steps.name: Verify WSIB or WCB clearance online
steps.description: The analyst looks up the firm's account in the WSIB eClearance service (or the provincial WCB portal), confirms the clearance is valid, records the expiry date and saves the certificate to the file.

control.basis: Workplace Safety and Insurance Act (Ontario): principal liable for a contractor's unpaid premiums and offence if construction work proceeds without a valid clearance; provincial WCB equivalents

next.condition: no valid clearance or account not in good standing

evidence.note: Clearances valid up to 90 days, online verification, principal's offence and fine up to $100,000.

steps.name: Check insurance certificates against requirements
steps.description: The analyst compares the broker's certificate with the company's minimums for general liability, automobile, and for some trades professional or pollution liability, and checks the additional insured wording and expiry dates.

error.defect_description: Additional insured or expiry date missed.

evidence.note: Minimum general liability ($2M) and automobile ($1-2M) certificates required; times and deficiency rate are estimates.

steps.name: Risk and insurance manager reviews the deficiency
steps.description: The risk and insurance manager decides whether a lower limit or different wording is acceptable for the trade's risk, needs an endorsement from the broker, or blocks the approval.

control.basis: Corporate insurance policy: minimum subcontractor insurance limits and additional insured requirements

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of Canadian general contractors.

steps.name: Review safety performance and safety program
steps.description: The regional safety manager reviews three years of lost-time and recordable injury rates, the WSIB experience rating against the industry rate, fatalities, ministry orders and fines, COR status and the safety program contents for the trade's hazards, and rates the firm.

error.defect_description: A weak safety record is rated acceptable because statistics are self-reported.

control.basis: OHSA constructor duty to ensure every employer on the project complies (Ontario OHSA s. 23) and company subcontractor safety prequalification policy

evidence.note: LTIFR and TRIFR per 200,000 hours, premium rate statements, fines and safety program checklist (Ketek); review by technical specialists on WCB details and safety statistics (gravelbc form); times are estimates.

steps.name: Analyse financial statements and propose a limit
steps.description: The analyst enters the last two or three years of financial statements into the scoring spreadsheet, calculates working capital, debt to equity and revenue trend, reads the bonding letter, and proposes a single-subcontract and aggregate limit.

error.defect_description: Limit set from unaudited statements that overstate working capital.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of Canadian general contractors.

steps.name: Check references and internal performance history
steps.description: The analyst reads post-job evaluations and any performance notices from the company's own projects, and calls two or three other contractors or owners named as references about schedule, quality, manpower and payment of their suppliers.

next.condition: requested limit above the analyst's authority or weak financials

evidence.note: Evaluation on performance and post-job reviews; time is an estimate.

steps.name: Treasury reviews financial capacity for a large limit
steps.description: The treasury manager reviews the statements and bonding letter for firms seeking large subcontracts, may call the trade's surety to confirm bonding capacity, and sets whether a performance bond or a lower limit is required.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of Canadian general contractors.

steps.name: Compile the scorecard and recommendation
steps.description: The analyst combines the safety, financial, insurance, reference and capability scores into the weighted scorecard and writes the recommendation: approve, approve with conditions (limit, bond, safety plan) or reject.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of Canadian general contractors.

steps.name: Approve the prequalification and limit
steps.description: The supply chain manager reviews the scorecard and approves, attaches conditions or rejects, so that the analyst who gathered the information is not the person who grants the limit.

control.basis: Procurement policy: subcontractor limits approved by a manager independent of the analyst

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of Canadian general contractors.

steps.name: Update the approved list and expiry dates
steps.description: The analyst records the approval, trades, regions, single and aggregate limits and the expiry dates of insurance, clearance and the prequalification itself in the database that estimators use to build bid lists.

error.defect_description: Limit or expiry date keyed incorrectly.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of Canadian general contractors.

steps.name: Set automatic expiry reminders
steps.description: The prequalification database schedules reminders to the subcontractor and analyst before the insurance certificate, WSIB clearance and annual prequalification expire.

evidence.note: Clearances expire on fixed quarterly dates, which makes scheduled reminders routine.

steps.name: Notify the subcontractor and estimators
steps.description: The analyst emails the approval letter with the limit and renewal date to the subcontractor and tells the requesting estimator that the firm can now be invited to bid.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of Canadian general contractors.

steps.name: Issue a conditional approval
steps.description: The analyst records the conditions (reduced limit, performance bond, site-specific safety plan or probation on the first job) in the database and sends the conditional approval letter to the subcontractor and estimator.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of Canadian general contractors.

steps.name: Notify the rejection and record reasons
steps.description: The analyst records the reasons in the database, sends a letter explaining which requirements were not met and when the firm may reapply, and informs the estimator who requested it.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of Canadian general contractors.

exceptions.name: Incomplete or expired documents
exceptions.description: The trade sends a package with missing statements or expired insurance or clearance certificates, and the analyst chases it one or more times before review can start.

exceptions.name: Insurance deficiency
exceptions.description: Limits or additional insured wording fall short and the risk and insurance manager decides whether to accept or require a revised certificate.

exceptions.name: Large limit needs treasury review
exceptions.description: A trade bidding mechanical, electrical or structural packages asks for a limit above the analyst's authority, so treasury reviews financial capacity and bonding.

exceptions.name: Urgent prequalification before a bid closes
exceptions.description: An estimator needs a new trade approved within days to have coverage on a package; the analyst and safety manager fast-track the file, which is when checks are most often shortened.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from request to decision

evidence.note: Author's estimate: one to two weeks for the trade to assemble documents, one or two chases for a large minority, and a few days each for safety and manager review; no published figure was found.
Clearances are valid for up to 90 days from the date of issue.

pain_points.description: Trades send incomplete packages or expired certificates, and chasing them is most of the elapsed time.

evidence.note: Organisation file and author's estimate; insurance and clearance certificates expire on fixed cycles.

pain_points.description: Safety review waits on regional safety managers whose main job is site safety, so files sit in their queue.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from the organisation's six regional safety managers covering about 220 sites.

pain_points.description: Clearances and insurance certificates expire after approval, so a trade on the approved list may be working without valid cover unless reminders are acted on.

evidence.note: Clearances last up to 90 days and must be valid for the whole job; the principal commits an offence otherwise.

pain_points.description: Injury statistics and financial statements are self-reported and often unaudited, so limits rest on information the analyst cannot verify.

evidence.note: Statistics are completed by the contractor on the questionnaire.

sources.title: Questions and answers: Clearances
sources.supports: Clearances are valid for up to 90 days from issue and most expire on 20 February, May, August and November; a valid clearance must be in place for the full length of the job; if construction work proceeds without one, the principal and the contractor both commit an offence (maximum fine $100,000 under the WSIA); principals can verify clearance numbers and search registered businesses online; WSIB issues a new clearance automatically if the account is in good standing.

sources.title: F211 Contractor Pre-Qualification Package (revision 13)
sources.supports: A Canadian contractor's 2021 prequalification package: contractors must prequalify before working on its sites; required documents are a safety manual table of contents, a current WCB clearance letter, three years of WCB premium rate statements with the industry rate, $2,000,000 general liability and $2,000,000 automobile liability insurance, a COR certificate if held, an environmental policy and a COVID-19 plan; questionnaire on lost-time and total recordable injury frequency (per 200,000 hours) for three years, fatalities, fines, hazard identification, safety program elements and critical work procedures; a vice-president can waive requirements after reviewing a contractor risk mitigation plan.

sources.title: Subcontractor Prequalification (form)
sources.publisher: gravelbc.ca (contractor's subcontractor form; company name not shown in the extracted text)
sources.supports: Subcontractors must complete the prequalification form and supporting documents before bidding; failure to submit excludes them from work; technical specialists review WCB details, safety statistics and performance and decide suitability for bidding; required WCB clearance, $2,000,000 general liability and $1,000,000 automobile liability certificates; safety registries listed (Avetta, ISN, ComplyWorks, COR); post-job safety performance reviews of all subcontractors.

assumptions: Volume includes annual renewals of already-approved trades as well as new firms; the organisation file's 40 to 90 a month appears to count only new firms.
Loaded costs and titles come from the organisation file (wage x 1.35 for salaried staff).
Roles needed but not listed for this process in the organisation file: risk-insurance-manager (insurance deficiencies) and treasury-manager (large limits).
Ongoing quarterly WSIB clearance checks before each subcontractor payment belong to subcontractor invoice payment, not to this process.
Approval shares (80% approved, 12% conditional, 6% rejected) are estimates; most firms that would fail never complete a submission.
The chase loop returns to the subcontractor wait step, so each chase re-samples the trade's response time of two to fourteen days.
